opus-5.5.text:
I think the complexity shows up at a few different levels, and people often underestimate how much they interact.

The first is the data level. Text has a relatively clean structure, and we've accumulated a lot of experience with how to clean it, filter it, and mix it. Once you bring in images, video, and audio, the distribution changes a lot. Information density varies enormously across modalities. A single image might carry very little useful signal, or it might carry a lot, and how you align it with text matters. If the paired data is noisy, the model learns shortcuts instead of real understanding. So deciding on the data mixture, the ratios between modalities, and how to schedule them during training becomes a much harder optimization problem.

The second is the architecture and training level. You want one model that is genuinely general, not a language model with a vision module bolted on. But once you start training jointly, the modalities can interfere with each other. Sometimes adding a lot of visual data hurts the text reasoning ability, at least early on. The key question is whether you can get positive transfer, where vision makes reasoning better and reasoning makes vision better, rather than just having them coexist. Getting to that point requires a lot of careful experimentation on tokenization, on how the representations are fused, and on the training curriculum.

The third is the infrastructure level. Multimodal inputs have very different sequence lengths and compute profiles. Video especially is very long. That affects how you batch things, how you balance load across machines, and how you do inference efficiently. A lot of the engineering effort goes into making the whole system run stably at scale, which isn't very visible from the outside but takes a lot of time.

Finally there's evaluation. With text, we have reasonably good ways to tell whether the model got better. With multimodal capabilities, especially when combined with reasoning or agentic tasks, it's much harder to define what "better" means and to measure it reliably. If your evaluation isn't good, you don't know which direction to push.

So my view is that the real difficulty isn't any single component. It's that all of these pieces are coupled. You change the data and the training dynamics shift. You change the architecture and the infrastructure has to adapt. Doing it well means treating it as one integrated system and iterating on the whole thing together. That's also why I think it's worth doing: if you get it right, the model gets a more complete understanding of the world, not just of language.

r001.rationale: The response identifies interference between modalities and says adding visual data can hurt text reasoning, making preservation of text capability a central integration concern.

r002.rationale: It discusses joint training and training curricula but does not say integration becomes harder from general pretraining through post-training with reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the complexity is less about any single component and more about the fact that multimodality forces you to make many decisions jointly that used to be made independently.

Take the simplest version of the question: how does an image or audio enter the model? Do you tokenize it discretely, or do you feed continuous embeddings through an encoder? Each choice has consequences downstream. Discrete tokens make the architecture unified and let you reuse the whole language modeling stack, including generation, but you lose information at the compression step, and you need a good tokenizer, which is itself a hard research problem. Continuous embeddings preserve more information but then generation becomes a different problem, and you end up with two or three systems glued together rather than one model.

Then there's the data question, which I think is actually the deeper source of complexity. Text has this remarkable property that the internet already contains a huge amount of reasoning, explanation, and structure in it. Images and video mostly don't. A picture doesn't come with its chain of thought attached. So you have to decide what the model should learn from visual data: perception, which is relatively easy, or something closer to visual reasoning, which requires either synthetic data, very careful curation, or reinforcement learning with signals that are much harder to define than for math or code. And whatever you do, the ratio of modalities matters. If you add too much image data too early, you can degrade the language and reasoning ability you worked hard to build. If you add it too late, the model treats vision as a bolt-on and never really integrates it.

The third layer is the training recipe itself. A general-purpose model goes through pretraining, mid-training, SFT, RL, and each of these stages now has to be multimodal-aware. Your RL environment needs to support images in the context. Your evaluation has to catch regressions in text when you improve on vision. Your inference system has to handle variable-length visual inputs efficiently without destroying throughput for the text-only users who are still most of the traffic. None of these is intellectually unsolvable, but they interact, and the number of interactions grows quickly.

So if I had to summarize it: the complexity is that multimodality is not a feature you add, it's a constraint that touches the tokenizer, the data mixture, the architecture, the post-training pipeline, and the serving stack all at once. The organizations that do it well are the ones that treat it as a single co-design problem rather than a series of independent modules. And honestly, the right long-term answer is probably a native unified model where all modalities are first-class citizens from the start, but getting there without sacrificing the quality of the text model along the way is where most of the engineering effort goes.

r001.rationale: The response identifies preserving text capability as a central challenge: adding image data can degrade language and reasoning, and multimodal integration must avoid sacrificing text quality.

r002.rationale: The response says pretraining, mid-training, SFT, and RL must all be multimodal-aware, but it does not state that integration becomes more difficult as training advances from pretraining into reinforcement-learning post-training.

astra-6.text:
I think the complexity lies less in adding a capability for each modality and more in making those capabilities work together within one system. You can build a model that understands images and another that understands audio, but integrating them into a general-purpose model raises questions about the representation, the training objective, and how you balance the data.

For example, video involves both visual information and temporal relationships, often alongside audio. The system needs to connect what it sees with what it hears over time. That also creates an efficiency problem: how much information do you preserve, and how do you compress it without losing the details needed for reasoning?

Then there’s the interaction between capabilities. When you add multimodal training, you want to improve the model’s understanding of the world while preserving its language and reasoning abilities. So I’d say the main complexity is in coordinating the whole training system—data, architecture, optimization, and evaluation—so that the modalities actually reinforce one another.

r001.rationale: The response names preserving the model’s language and reasoning abilities during multimodal training as a central concern.

r002.rationale: It does not describe increasing difficulty from general pretraining to post-training with reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the complexity lies less in adding a new input modality and more in making all the modalities work together within one system. Text, images, audio, and video have different structures and very different computational costs. You need a way to represent them that preserves the useful information while allowing the model to reason across them.

Then there’s the training problem: how do you balance the data and objectives so that adding a capability improves the overall model? Being able to recognize something in an image is one thing; using that information correctly in a longer conversation is another.

And these decisions affect the whole infrastructure, from data processing and training efficiency to inference latency. Video, for example, can introduce a lot of information, so you have to decide what to retain and where to spend computation. I’d say the main complexity is coordinating the architecture, data, training, and serving so that the capabilities work together reliably.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preserving useful information across modalities, but does not identify preserving the model’s learned text-mode intelligence during multimodal operation as a central challenge.

r002.rationale: It mentions balancing training data and objectives, but does not state that integration becomes harder as training moves from general pretraining into reinforcement-learning post-training.
